analogy.p: Imagine a motorist driving along a road with a fixed supply of energy to spend. On the open road (temperature rising) the energy goes into speeding up: the car's kinetic energy increases. At the border the car must stop and pay a toll (latent heat) before it can cross; during that time the car does not get any faster, but the money is gone and the car ends up on the other side (new state). The toll for a bigger border crossing (boiling) is much bigger than for a small one (melting). Where it breaks down: a toll is a one-off payment lost forever, whereas latent heat is not lost; it is stored as potential energy and given back when the substance freezes or condenses.
analogy.t: Paying a toll at a border

bullets: **Latent heat** is the energy transferred when a substance changes state; the word latent means hidden, because the temperature does not show any change.
During a change of state the energy supplied changes the **energy stored (internal energy)** of the substance but **not its temperature**.
The substance stays at its **melting point** (solid to liquid) or **boiling point** (liquid to gas) until the whole change of state is complete.
A change of state is a **physical change**, not a chemical change: the substance is the same, so it can be reversed and the mass is conserved.
This topic follows directly from **internal energy** and **specific heat capacity** (the previous points) and leads on to **gas pressure**.
Typical exam use: a calculation with E = mL (2 to 3 marks), a graph question (explain a flat section, 2 to 4 marks), or a compare-the-two-quantities question.
core.h: What latent heat is and what the specification asks
core.p: When you heat a substance, the energy you supply does not always make it hotter. At a **change of state** (melting, freezing, boiling, condensing) the temperature stays **constant** even though energy is still being transferred. The energy needed (or released) for a substance to change state is called **latent heat**. The specification expects you to define **specific latent heat**, use **energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat**, distinguish **specific latent heat of fusion** from **specific latent heat of vaporisation**, interpret **heating and cooling graphs** that include changes of state, and **distinguish specific heat capacity from specific latent heat**.

bullets: **Temperature** is a measure of the **average kinetic energy** of the particles: faster particles on average means a higher temperature.
When the temperature **rises** (and no change of state occurs), the energy supplied increases the **kinetic energy** of the particles.

During a **change of state**, the energy supplied increases the **potential energy** of the particles as they are pulled further apart against the attractive forces; the average kinetic energy does **not** change, so the temperature is constant.

Gaining potential energy means the particles are **less tightly held**: in a solid they are in fixed positions; in a liquid they can move past each other; in a gas the forces between them are negligible.
So **energy in = energy stored**: heating a solid at its melting point raises its internal energy but the particles end up as a liquid at the **same temperature**.
Because the internal energy of a gas at the same temperature as its liquid is greater, you can say a gas at 100 °C has more internal energy than the same mass of water at 100 °C.
Always write which energy store changes: say the **potential energy of the particles** increases, not just that energy is 'used up'.
core.h: Internal energy: why temperature and state are linked to different energy stores
core.p: Every substance is made of particles. The **internal energy** is the **total kinetic energy plus the total potential energy** of all the particles in the system. The **kinetic energy** is due to the random motion of particles (vibrating in solids, moving around in liquids and gases). The **potential energy** is due to the forces (bonds) between particles, which depends on how far apart they are. Heating a substance transfers energy to its particles, and what that energy does depends on whether the substance is changing state.

bullets: Definition to learn: **specific latent heat = energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance, with no change in temperature**.
Unit: **J/kg**; for water you often see it written as **kJ/kg** or in standard form, for example 3.34 × 10^5 J/kg.
Each substance has its **own** values of specific latent heat, depending on the strength of the forces between its particles.
There are **two** values for each substance: one for **melting/freezing (fusion)** and one for **boiling/condensing (vaporisation)**.
The same value is used for the reverse change: the energy **released** when a liquid freezes equals the energy **absorbed** when the solid melts (same mass).
Latent heat is an **energy transfer to or from the substance**: it is found by measuring energy supplied by a heater (electrical energy E = P t) or the energy removed by cooling.
The word 'specific' always means **per kilogram**: specific heat capacity is per kilogram per °C, specific latent heat is per kilogram only.
core.p: The **specific latent heat** of a substance is the **amount of energy required to change the state of one kilogram of the substance with no change in temperature**. This is the exact wording the specification uses, and mark schemes reward each key part: 'one kilogram', 'change of state' and 'no change in temperature'. It is called specific because it refers to **1 kg**, so it lets you compare different substances fairly regardless of the amount you have. Its unit is **joules per kilogram (J/kg)**.

bullets: **Fusion** = melting: solid to liquid at the **melting point**. The reverse (freezing) releases the same energy per kilogram.
**Vaporisation** = boiling: liquid to gas at the **boiling point**. The reverse (condensing) releases the same energy per kilogram.
Melting needs energy to **loosen** the particles from fixed positions; boiling needs energy to **completely separate** them.
Condensing steam to water releases a lot of energy, which is why **steam burns are worse** than burns from boiling water at the same temperature.
Sublimation (solid to gas directly) is not in the specification, so you do not need a latent-heat value for it.
When a substance **freezes or condenses**, energy is transferred **to the surroundings** and the temperature stays constant while it changes state.
Exam hint: 'latent heat of **fusion**' goes with **solid and liquid**; 'latent heat of **vaporisation**' goes with **liquid and gas**.
core.h: Fusion and vaporisation: the two types
core.p: The specification names two kinds of specific latent heat. The **specific latent heat of fusion** is the energy needed to change **1 kg of a substance from solid to liquid** with no temperature change. The **specific latent heat of vaporisation** is the energy needed to change **1 kg of a substance from liquid to vapour (gas)** with no temperature change. Because the particles are being pulled apart against attractive forces, each change needs energy to be **supplied**, and the reverse change **releases** the same amount.

bullets: **E = m L** where E is energy in joules (J), m is mass in kilograms (kg), L is specific latent heat in joules per kilogram (J/kg).
Rearranged for mass: **m = E ÷ L**. Rearranged for specific latent heat: **L = E ÷ m**.
Convert grams to kilograms first: 250 g = **0.250 kg**. Convert kJ to J if needed: 334 kJ/kg = **334 000 J/kg**.
Use the correct L: **fusion** for melting/freezing, **vaporisation** for boiling/condensing. A common error is to use the wrong one.
There is **no temperature change term** in E = m L, because the temperature is constant during the change of state.
If a question gives power and time, find the energy first using **E = P t** (energy = power × time) and then use E = mL. Electrical energy is also E = V I t.
Check your answer is sensible: boiling should need about **seven times** more energy than melting for water (2.26 × 10^6 ÷ 3.34 × 10^5 is about 6.8).
Give units: J, or kJ if you divide by 1000 (state the unit clearly).
core.p: The energy for a change of state is calculated using **energy for a change of state (J) = mass (kg) × specific latent heat (J/kg)**, written **E = m L**. Check whether your exam gives this equation on the equation sheet, but either way you must be able to use it and **rearrange** it confidently. Multiply the mass of the substance that changes state by the correct specific latent heat (fusion or vaporisation), and give the answer in joules.

bullets: Water: **L(fusion) = 334 000 J/kg**; **L(vaporisation) = 2 260 000 J/kg** (values may differ slightly between exam papers; always use the one given).
In melting the particles stay **close together** (most bonds remain, just loosened); in boiling the particles move from touching to **far apart**, a much larger change in potential energy.
The large volume increase when liquid becomes gas means the vapour must **push back the atmosphere**, which takes extra energy.
Substances with **strong forces between particles** (like water with hydrogen bonds) usually have large latent heats; this is why water is excellent for cooling.
Sweating cools you because the liquid that **evaporates** takes latent heat from your skin.
Ice packs and cold drinks with ice work well because melting 1 kg of ice at 0 °C absorbs 334 kJ without the ice getting warmer.
Steam in a power station or a steam iron carries a large amount of energy because of the latent heat of vaporisation it releases when it condenses.
core.h: Values for water and why vaporisation needs much more energy
core.p: For water the specific latent heat of **fusion** is about **334 000 J/kg** (3.34 × 10^5 J/kg) and the specific latent heat of **vaporisation** is about **2 260 000 J/kg** (2.26 × 10^6 J/kg). Exam questions normally give the value you need, so you do not have to memorise them, but you should understand the comparison. Vaporisation needs much more energy per kilogram than fusion for two reasons: in boiling the particles must be separated **completely** (all the attractive forces overcome), and the gas also does work in **pushing back the atmosphere** as it expands.

bullets: Start (low temperature): the substance is a **solid**, warming up, so the line slopes upward.
First flat section: **melting**. The temperature at which it is flat is the **melting point**. Solid and liquid are both present.
Second sloping section: the **liquid** warming up.

Second flat section: **boiling**. The temperature here is the **boiling point**; liquid and gas are both present. This flat section is **longer** than the melting one because vaporisation needs more energy (constant power).
Final sloping section: the **gas** warming up.
The **length of a flat section** is proportional to the energy needed: longer plateau = larger latent heat for the same mass and power.
The **gradient** of a sloping section depends on the specific heat capacity: a steeper line means a **lower** specific heat capacity for the same mass and power.
If the graph uses energy supplied on the x-axis, the horizontal width of the plateau = **m L**.
Quote data: read the melting and boiling temperatures from the y-axis and say what is happening in each section.
core.p: A **heating curve** plots temperature (y-axis) against time (x-axis) for a substance heated at a constant rate. The graph has **sloping sections** and **flat (horizontal) sections**. On the sloping sections the substance is in one state and its temperature is rising: the energy supplied increases the **kinetic energy** of the particles. On the flat sections the substance is changing state: the energy supplied increases the **potential energy** of the particles, so the temperature does not change. Reading these correctly is a very common exam skill.

bullets: Flat sections occur at the **freezing point** (same temperature as the melting point) and the **condensing point** (same as the boiling point) for a pure substance.
During freezing, energy is **transferred to the surroundings** as the particles settle into fixed positions and their potential energy decreases.

A **pure substance** has a sharp, fixed melting/boiling point, so its graph has clean flat sections; an **impure substance** or mixture changes state over a range of temperatures, so there is no flat plateau.
Cooling graphs often curve rather than being straight because the **rate of cooling decreases** as the substance gets closer to room temperature (the temperature difference is smaller).

Exam question: 'Explain why the temperature stays constant between 5 and 9 minutes.' Answer: **it is changing state; energy is being released (or supplied) and this changes the potential energy of the particles, not their kinetic energy**.
Identify the state at each point by reading the graph left to right (or right to left for a cooling curve) and checking above/below the melting and boiling points.
core.p: A **cooling curve** shows temperature against time as a gas is cooled to a solid. It is the heating curve in reverse: the gas cools (sloping down), **condenses** (flat), the liquid cools (sloping down), then **freezes** (flat) and the solid continues to cool. During the flat sections the substance is **releasing** energy to the surroundings, but its temperature does not fall because the particles are forming bonds and **losing potential energy**, while their average kinetic energy stays the same.

bullets: **Specific heat capacity (c)**: energy needed to raise the temperature of **1 kg** of a substance by **1 °C**. Unit **J/kg °C**. Equation **ΔE = m c Δθ**.
**Specific latent heat (L)**: energy needed to change the **state** of **1 kg** of a substance with **no temperature change**. Unit **J/kg**. Equation **E = m L**.
With c: the **kinetic energy** of the particles changes and the temperature changes. With L: the **potential energy** changes and the temperature is constant.
On a heating graph, c is linked to the **sloping** parts; L is linked to the **flat** parts.
c has a temperature change in its equation; L does **not**.
Never use c for a section where the substance is changing state, and never use L for a section where the temperature is changing.
Memory aid: **c = change in temperature; L = change in state (Latent = Level line)**.
Both quantities are properties of the substance: different substances have different values, and both depend on the particle forces and arrangement.
core.h: Specific latent heat compared with specific heat capacity
core.p: The specification explicitly asks you to **distinguish** these two ideas. Specific heat capacity is about **changing the temperature** of a substance **without** changing state; specific latent heat is about **changing the state** **without** changing temperature. Both are energy per kilogram, but the first also includes 'per degree Celsius'.

bullets: Step 1: sketch the heating curve for the temperatures given and mark each stage.
Step 2: for each **sloping** section calculate m c Δθ using the c for that **state** (ice, water and steam have different values).
Step 3: for each **flat** section calculate m L using fusion or vaporisation as appropriate.
Step 4: **add** all the stages to get the total energy, then convert to kJ or find time using t = E ÷ P if power is given.
Check units at each stage: mass in **kg**, Δθ in °C, c in J/kg °C, L in J/kg.
If the system is not perfectly insulated, the **actual** energy supplied is greater than the calculated value because of energy lost to the surroundings.
Show each stage on a separate line to gain method marks even if you make an arithmetic slip.
Example in the worked section: 0.20 kg of ice at −10 °C to water at 20 °C.
core.p: Harder questions ask for the **total energy** to take a substance through several stages, for example ice at −10 °C to water at 20 °C. Break the problem into stages, and for each stage decide whether the **temperature is changing** (use ΔE = m c Δθ) or the **state is changing** (use E = m L). Then **add** all the energies. Draw a quick sketch of the heating curve first to see how many sloping and flat sections you need.

bullets: **Melting ice:** place crushed ice at 0 °C in a funnel with an immersion heater, with a beaker underneath on a balance to collect the water; run the heater for a measured time.
Use a **control funnel** with ice but no heater, to measure and subtract the mass of ice that melts from the warm room.
Calculate energy supplied: **E = P t** (power × time) or read it from a **joulemeter**; the mass melted m = mass of water collected (heater funnel) minus control funnel.
Then **L = E ÷ m**; the result is usually **higher or lower** than the true value because of energy exchanges with the surroundings.
**Boiling water:** heat water to boiling on a balance and record the **mass lost** over a measured time at a steady power; L = E ÷ mass lost.
**Sources of error:** energy lost to surroundings (insulate the container), energy gained from the room, ice not at 0 °C, drips still on the ice, heater not fully immersed.
**Safety:** keep electrical connections away from water, take care with hot steam and boiling water, use a heat-proof mat.
**Improving accuracy:** insulate, repeat and average, use crushed ice, wait until the water is dripping at a steady rate before starting timing.
**Variables:** independent: time or energy; dependent: mass of ice melted or water boiled; control: power of heater, starting temperature, type of substance.
core.h: Investigating latent heat in the laboratory
core.p: A typical investigation measures the specific latent heat of fusion of ice or vaporisation of water using an **electric heater** and a **joulemeter** (or power supply and stopwatch) to find the energy supplied. This is not a named AQA required practical, but the method and its evaluation are fair game in the exam. The key idea is to measure the **mass** of substance that changes state for a measured **energy**, then calculate **L = E ÷ m**.

bullets: **Refrigerators and air conditioners:** a liquid refrigerant evaporates inside the cold compartment, absorbing latent heat, then condenses outside, releasing it.
**Sweating and evaporation:** the most energetic particles leave the liquid, which takes energy away from the skin; this cools the body.
**Steam burns:** steam at 100 °C condenses on skin, releasing 2.26 × 10^6 J per kg, much more than the same mass of water at 100 °C cooling.
**Ice in drinks:** melting ice absorbs energy from the drink without warming up, so the drink cools down.
**Link to energy stores:** the thermal store changes without the temperature changing; the energy is in the **internal energy** of the substance.
**Link to power:** P = E ÷ t, so longer plateaus on the heating graph mean more energy at constant power.
**Link to density and particle model:** the change in volume at boiling reflects particles being far apart.
**Link to gas pressure (next points):** once a substance is a gas, its particles collide with container walls to create pressure; heating gas raises the temperature and pressure.

**Higher tier extension:** when a mixture of ice and water is at 0 °C, adding energy melts ice without changing temperature, which is why a mixture of ice and water stays at 0 °C until all the ice is gone.
core.h: Real-life applications and links to other topics
core.p: Latent heat appears in everyday life and links to many other parts of GCSE Physics. Being able to use the idea in an unfamiliar context is what separates grade 7 to 9 answers from lower ones. In every case the logic is the same: **energy is transferred to or from the substance while its temperature stays constant, because the potential energy of the particles changes.**

exam: **State/identify (1 mark):** give the definition or name the type, e.g. 'fusion is solid to liquid', 'vaporisation is liquid to gas'.
**Define specific latent heat (2 marks):** one mark for 'energy to change the state of 1 kg' and one for 'with no change in temperature'.
**Calculation (2-3 marks):** write E = m L, substitute with mass in kg, give the answer with units (J or kJ). One mark each for equation, substitution and answer.
**Rearranging (3 marks):** show m = E ÷ L or L = E ÷ m first, then substitute, then answer with units. Include a power-time step (E = P t) if the energy is not given directly.

**Graph explain (2-4 marks):** say (1) it is changing state, (2) energy is still being supplied/released, (3) this changes the potential energy of the particles, (4) the average kinetic energy / temperature does not change.
**Graph read (1-2 marks):** quote the temperature of the plateau from the y-axis for the melting or boiling point; compare plateau lengths for the energy needed.
**Compare c and L (3-4 marks):** link c to temperature change and L to state change, give both units, and name the energy store changes (kinetic vs potential).
**Why is L(vaporisation) bigger than L(fusion)? (2 marks):** particles must be completely separated against all attractive forces, and the gas pushes back the atmosphere.
**6-mark answers:** structure it: stage 1 (solid heating), stage 2 (melting), stage 3 (liquid heating), stage 4 (boiling); use correct equations and show a final total.
**Command words:** 'calculate' = work out with numbers; 'explain' = give reasons using the particle model; 'compare' = give similarities and differences.
**Always** give units and use the right significant figures (usually 2 or 3 s.f. matching the data given).

mistakes.r: The energy is being transferred and increases the potential energy of the particles (breaking bonds); the temperature stays the same because the average kinetic energy does not change.
mistakes.w: The temperature stays the same because the energy is not being used.

mistakes.r: During a change of state the particles gain potential energy, not kinetic energy; they move faster only when the temperature rises.
mistakes.w: Latent heat makes the particles move faster.

mistakes.r: Use E = m L for a change of state; there is no temperature change so Δθ = 0 would give zero.
mistakes.w: Using m c Δθ for the flat part of a graph.

mistakes.r: Fusion = solid and liquid; vaporisation = liquid and gas. Match the L to the change that occurs.
mistakes.w: Using fusion for boiling (or vaporisation for melting).

mistakes.r: Convert to kilograms before using E = m L (e.g. 500 g = 0.500 kg).
It is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of the substance with no change in temperature; include 'one kilogram' and 'no change in temperature'.
mistakes.w: Specific latent heat is the energy needed to melt a substance.

mistakes.r: A change of state is happening; energy is being transferred and the potential energy of the particles is changing.
mistakes.w: The flat part means nothing is happening.

mistakes.r: Boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point; evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature below the boiling point.
mistakes.w: Boiling is the same as evaporation.

summary: Know that the energy supplied at a change of state changes the internal energy (potential energy of particles) but not the temperature, define specific latent heat of fusion and vaporisation, use E = m L, interpret heating and cooling graphs and distinguish specific latent heat from specific heat capacity. This matters because it explains plateaus on graphs and underpins many energy calculations.

terms.d: The energy transferred when a substance changes state, without a change in temperature.
The amount of energy required to change the state of one kilogram of the substance with no change in temperature.
The amount of energy required to change 1 kg of a substance from a solid to a liquid with no change in temperature.
The amount of energy required to change 1 kg of a substance from a liquid to a vapour with no change in temperature.
A physical change between solid, liquid and gas (melting, freezing, boiling, condensing); the mass is conserved.
The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles that make up a system.
The temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid; equal to the freezing point for a pure substance.
The temperature at which a liquid changes to a gas throughout the liquid; equal to the condensing point for a pure substance.
The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius.
Energy due to the movement of particles; the average kinetic energy determines the temperature.
Energy stored because of the forces between particles; it increases when particles are pulled further apart.
A flat section of a temperature-time graph where the temperature is constant, showing a change of state.
The unit of energy; one joule is the energy transferred when a force of one newton moves an object one metre in the direction of the force.
A single element or compound with no other substances mixed in; it has a sharp melting and boiling point.

worked.q: The specific latent heat of fusion of water is 334 000 J/kg. Calculate the energy needed to melt 0.50 kg of ice at 0 °C. (2 marks)
steps: Write the equation: E = m L.

worked.q: A 3.0 kW kettle element is switched on for 5.0 minutes while the water is boiling. The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.26 × 10^6 J/kg. Assuming all the energy boils water, calculate the mass of water turned to steam. (4 marks)
steps: Time in seconds: 5.0 min = 300 s; power = 3000 W.
Rearrange E = m L to m = E ÷ L.

worked.ans: 87 800 J (87.8 kJ). The melting stage uses most of the energy.
worked.q: Calculate the total energy needed to change 0.20 kg of ice at −10 °C into water at 20 °C. Specific heat capacity of ice = 2100 J/kg °C; specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kg °C; specific latent heat of fusion = 334 000 J/kg. (6 marks)
steps: Stage 1 (warm ice to 0 °C): ΔE = m c Δθ = 0.20 × 2100 × 10 = 4200 J.
